LETTER:
To the Road Authority
Subject: Request for safety improvement at Ring Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school monitored the Ring Road crossing outside the school from video for 20.8 minutes (1248.0 s). In that time we recorded 32 crossings and 21 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 55.2 km/h. Many pupils said they felt frightened crossing because drivers seldom slowed down.

The analysis found 3 serious near-misses (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 1 close pass (1.5-3.0 s). Of the 4 interactions, 2 were person-first and 2 were vehicle-first.

One serious near-miss had a PET of 1.3 s with a car at 57.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed, the death risk is 15.1% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
Another serious near-miss had a PET of 1.3 s with a car at 36.4 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed, the death risk is 2.6%.
A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.8 s with a bus at 14.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed, the death risk is 0.4%.
One close pass had a PET of 2.5 s with a van at 30.2 km/h.

For engineering context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 (92 pedestrians and 61 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 20.8 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice: 1.3x the true count in our drone test). Also, 46.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps in total and 4 of them 12 s or more and longest 86.3 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We can share the video and Crossing Watch measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

The modelled adult death risk if hit by the car front for that impact is 1.6%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h. A close pass had a car at 14.6 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 2.6 s.

PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 9.3, with 3 pedestrian crossings and 19 moving vehicles counted. 50.9% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 10 gaps, 3 of them 12 s or more, longest 81.6 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce speeds and protect pupils.

We are happy to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write regarding safety outside our school at Lake View Road crossing.

We measured traffic from video for 2.4 minutes. In that time there were 5 pedestrian crossings and 6 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 50.9 km/h. The counts above are past the threshold the road code sets for a zebra crossing.

We recorded 5 serious near-misses. Serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart.

One serious near-miss had a PET of 0.0 s with a motorcycle travelling at 45.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 5.5%.
One serious near-miss had a PET of 1.1 s with a car travelling at 38.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 3.1%.
One serious near-miss had a PET of 0.7 s with a car travelling at 34.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 2.3%.
One serious near-miss had a PET of 1.4 s with a van travelling at 23.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.9%.
One serious near-miss had a PET of 1.0 s with a motorcycle travelling at 16.4 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.4%.

Risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosen and Sander 2009.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and protect pedestrians.

We are willing to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority,

Subject: Request for safety improvements at Canal Road crossing

We write as the school using the Canal Road crossing. Video-based measurements over 36.1 minutes recorded 40 crossings and 6 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 54.0 km/h. The death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

The analysis found 1 serious near-miss and 0 close passes, where serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass means 1.5 s to 3.0 s. In that serious case the vehicle arrived first in 1 of 1 event. The worst case had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s.
It involved a motorcycle at 46.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 6.1% from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+ car fronts. At a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with a modelled adult death risk of 0.0%.

Engineering context from the same video: PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 66 pedestrians and 10 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 36.1 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one twice at 1.3x the true count in a drone test. 43.0% of time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 2 gaps of 6 s or more, 1 of them 12 s or more, longest 15.2 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you provide a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and give priority to pedestrians.

We would be pleased to share the video and data file reviewed for your verification and to discuss the matter further.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write regarding the Garden Road crossing outside our school. A Crossing Watch analysis (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) of 3.9 minutes of video recorded 9 pedestrian crossings and 20 vehicles with an 85th percentile speed of 53.6 km/h. Every person in these near-misses was a pupil of our school.

The review found 2 serious near-misses where pedestrian and moving vehicle were on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and 3 close passes of 1.5 s to 3.0 s.

The most severe serious near-miss involved a bus at 46.8 km/h with a gap of 0.0 s.
If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 6.4% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.
A second serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 30.9 km/h with a gap of 0.7 s.
If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 1.6%, compared to 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.
A further close pass involved a car at 48.5 km/h with a gap of 1.6 s and 5.9% adult death risk if hit by a car front.

PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this sample is 3.9 minutes, so they cannot be used reliably. The video also showed 42.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, in 3 gaps, 2 of them 12 s or more, longest 27.2 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location and are happy to share the video for your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority
Subject: Request for safety improvement at Ring Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school monitored the Ring Road crossing outside the school from video for 20.8 minutes (1248.0 s). In that time we recorded 32 crossings and 21 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 55.2 km/h. One near-miss ended with the vehicle hitting the person crossing.

The analysis found 3 serious near-misses (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 1 close pass (1.5-3.0 s). Of the 4 interactions, 2 were person-first and 2 were vehicle-first.

One serious near-miss had a PET of 1.3 s with a car at 57.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed, the death risk is 15.1% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
Another serious near-miss had a PET of 1.3 s with a car at 36.4 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed, the death risk is 2.6%.
A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.8 s with a bus at 14.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed, the death risk is 0.4%.
One close pass had a PET of 2.5 s with a van at 30.2 km/h.

For engineering context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 (92 pedestrians and 61 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 20.8 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice: 1.3x the true count in our drone test). Also, 46.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps in total and 4 of them 12 s or more and longest 86.3 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We can share the video and Crossing Watch measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

We write regarding the safety of the crossing outside our school on Market Street.

We arranged a video-based Crossing Watch for 36.4 minutes (2184.0 s). In that time 35 crossings and 39 vehicles were observed. 6 of 35 crossings (1 in 5.8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 35 crossings (1 in 12) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 6.6-33.6% and 1.8-23.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile speed was 57.4 km/h. The drivers involved were speeding because they were late for work.

By definition a serious near-miss is less than 1.5 s apart and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s apart.
One serious near-miss had a PET of 0.7 s with a car at 57.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 14.9% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+).
A second serious near-miss had a PET of 1.0 s with a van at 47.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 6.6%.
A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.5 s with a car at 39.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 3.3%.
A close pass had a PET of 1.8 s with a car at 21.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.3%.
A further close pass had a PET of 2.7 s with a van at 59.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front the recorded death risk is 0.0%.
At a 20 km/h limit the modelled adult death risks for these events would fall to 0.0%, 0.0%, 0.6%, 0.0% and 0.0% respectively.

In engineering terms, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, from 58 pedestrians and 64 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 36.4 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour. 69.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 10 such gaps, 1 of them 12 s or more and the longest 56.1 s; the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

Given these measurements we request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We are willing to share the video and tracking data for your review and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

We write regarding the safety of the crossing outside our school on Market Street.

We arranged a video-based Crossing Watch for 36.4 minutes (2184.0 s). In that time 35 crossings and 39 vehicles were observed. 6 of 35 crossings (1 in 5.8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 35 crossings (1 in 12) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 6.6-33.6% and 1.8-23.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile speed was 57.4 km/h.

By definition a serious near-miss is less than 1.5 s apart and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s apart.
One serious near-miss had a PET of 0.7 s with a car at 57.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 14.9% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+).
A second serious near-miss had a PET of 1.0 s with a van at 47.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 6.6%.
A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.5 s with a car at 39.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 3.3%.
A close pass had a PET of 1.8 s with a car at 21.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.3%.
A further close pass had a PET of 2.7 s with a van at 59.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front the recorded death risk is 0.0%.
At a 20 km/h limit the modelled adult death risks for these events would fall to 0.0%, 0.0%, 0.6%, 0.0% and 0.0% respectively.

In engineering terms, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, from 58 pedestrians and 64 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 36.4 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour. 69.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 10 such gaps, 1 of them 12 s or more and the longest 56.1 s; the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

Given these measurements we request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We are willing to share the video and tracking data for your review and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Ring Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school monitored the Ring Road crossing outside the school from video for 20.8 minutes (1248.0 s). In that time we recorded 32 crossings and 21 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 55.2 km/h. These figures come from a single recording and may differ on other days.

The analysis found 3 serious near-misses (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 1 close pass (1.5-3.0 s). Of the 4 interactions, 2 were person-first and 2 were vehicle-first.

Another serious near-miss had a PET of 1.3 s with a car at 36.4 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed, the death risk is 2.6%.
A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.8 s with a bus at 14.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed, the death risk is 0.4%.
One close pass had a PET of 2.5 s with a van at 30.2 km/h.

For engineering context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 (92 pedestrians and 61 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 20.8 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice: 1.3x the true count in our drone test). We request you install a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We can share the video and Crossing Watch measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

One serious near-miss had a time gap of 0.8 s with a car at 30.5 km/h; for an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 1.5%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.

Another serious near-miss had a time gap of 1.3 s with a van at 16.5 km/h; for an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.4%, compared with 0.4% at 16.5 km/h.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We write concerning the crossing outside our school at Cedar Lane crossing. A video survey of 43.5 minutes (2610.0 s) recorded 22 crossings and 15 vehicles.

Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 2.9-34.9% and 1.1-29.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

A second serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s and involved a bus at 12.0 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.3%.

Also, 49.9% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 10 gaps, 4 of them 12 s or more, and the longest 84.8 s; the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We would be pleased to share the video and data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority,

We write concerning the crossing outside our school at Brook Street crossing.

We arranged video monitoring using SAM tracking with road-plane geometry. In 17.4 minutes we recorded 20 pedestrian crossings and 24 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 44.9 km/h. There were 2 serious near-misses where pedestrian and moving vehicle were on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 4 close passes between 1.5 s and 3.0 s.

The most severe event had a post-encroachment time of 0.7 s and involved a motorcycle. That motorcycle was travelling at 37.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 2.8%.

A second serious event had a post-encroachment time of 0.5 s and involved a car. That car was travelling at 17.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 0.5%.

A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.6 s and involved a bus. That bus was travelling at 22.4 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 0.6%.

A further close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.8 s and involved a motorcycle. That motorcycle was travelling at 22.8 km/h.

A final close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.5 s and involved a bus. That bus was travelling at 30.8 km/h. All risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosén & Sander 2009.

Engineering review noted PV² of 0.0 x 10^8 based on 69 pedestrians and 83 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 17.4 minutes of video, while a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can double-count. It also noted 56.4% of time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with 5 such gaps and longest 11.1 s, though the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with a speed table to reduce speeds and provide protected crossing time.

We are happy to share the video and underlying measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request to make the crossing outside the school safer - Bridge Street crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write regarding the safety of the crossing outside our school on Bridge Street.

Crossing Watch measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) for 33.9 minutes recorded 24 crossings and 23 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 51.2 km/h. Several children have been hurt at this crossing since the term began.

In that period 6 of 24 crossings (1 in 4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 24 crossings (1 in 8) were within 1.5 s, classified as serious.

Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 9.8-46.7% for within 3 s and 2.7-32.4% for within 1.5 s (Clopper-Pearson), and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The worst near-misses were as follows. One serious near-miss had a PET of 1.2 s with a car at 49.3 km/h and an adult death risk of 7.9% if hit. Another serious near-miss had a PET of 1.1 s with a motorcycle at 38.9 km/h and an adult death risk of 3.2% if hit. A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.2 s with a car at 25.0 km/h and an adult death risk of 0.9% if hit. One close pass had a PET of 1.9 s with a car at 13.5 km/h. A further close pass had a PET of 2.8 s with a car at 33.3 km/h. Death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

For context, PV² was estimated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 42 pedestrians and 41 vehicles an hour scaled from 33.9 minutes of video, with the caveat that broken tracks can count one person twice at 1.3x the true count in a drone test and a formal check counts the full peak hour. 46.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 gaps and 9 of them 12 s or more and longest 39.1 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We would be pleased to share the Crossing Watch recording and measurements for your review and to discuss the site further.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request to make the crossing outside the school safer - Bridge Street crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write regarding the safety of the crossing outside our school on Bridge Street.

Crossing Watch measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) for 33.9 minutes recorded 24 crossings and 23 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 51.2 km/h. Children hit at these speeds face a far higher risk of death than adults.

In that period 6 of 24 crossings (1 in 4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 24 crossings (1 in 8) were within 1.5 s, classified as serious.

Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 9.8-46.7% for within 3 s and 2.7-32.4% for within 1.5 s (Clopper-Pearson), and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The worst near-misses were as follows. One serious near-miss had a PET of 1.2 s with a car at 49.3 km/h and an adult death risk of 7.9% if hit. Another serious near-miss had a PET of 1.1 s with a motorcycle at 38.9 km/h and an adult death risk of 3.2% if hit. A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.2 s with a car at 25.0 km/h and an adult death risk of 0.9% if hit. One close pass had a PET of 1.9 s with a car at 13.5 km/h. A further close pass had a PET of 2.8 s with a car at 33.3 km/h. Death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

For context, PV² was estimated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 42 pedestrians and 41 vehicles an hour scaled from 33.9 minutes of video, with the caveat that broken tracks can count one person twice at 1.3x the true count in a drone test and a formal check counts the full peak hour. 46.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 gaps and 9 of them 12 s or more and longest 39.1 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We would be pleased to share the Crossing Watch recording and measurements for your review and to discuss the site further.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request to make the crossing outside the school safer - Bridge Street crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write regarding the safety of the crossing outside our school on Bridge Street.

Crossing Watch measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) for 33.9 minutes recorded 24 crossings and 23 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 51.2 km/h. The closest of these passes was in fact a collision.

In that period 6 of 24 crossings (1 in 4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 24 crossings (1 in 8) were within 1.5 s, classified as serious.

Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 9.8-46.7% for within 3 s and 2.7-32.4% for within 1.5 s (Clopper-Pearson), and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The worst near-misses were as follows. One serious near-miss had a PET of 1.2 s with a car at 49.3 km/h and an adult death risk of 7.9% if hit. Another serious near-miss had a PET of 1.1 s with a motorcycle at 38.9 km/h and an adult death risk of 3.2% if hit. A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.2 s with a car at 25.0 km/h and an adult death risk of 0.9% if hit. One close pass had a PET of 1.9 s with a car at 13.5 km/h. A further close pass had a PET of 2.8 s with a car at 33.3 km/h. Death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

For context, PV² was estimated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 42 pedestrians and 41 vehicles an hour scaled from 33.9 minutes of video, with the caveat that broken tracks can count one person twice at 1.3x the true count in a drone test and a formal check counts the full peak hour. 46.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 gaps and 9 of them 12 s or more and longest 39.1 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We would be pleased to share the Crossing Watch recording and measurements for your review and to discuss the site further.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Garden Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school asked for a video review of Garden Road crossing. Measurements were made by Crossing Watch using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time over 18.1 minutes, which is 1086.0 s, during which 11 crossings and 26 vehicles were observed.

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write regarding safety outside our school at Lake View Road crossing.

We measured traffic from video for 2.4 minutes. In that time there were 5 pedestrian crossings and 6 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 50.9 km/h. The closest of these near-misses was the fault of Mr. Tarun Mehra, who runs the tea stall.

For context on engineering assessment, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 2.4. In the period recorded, 61.9% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed.

We recorded 5 serious near-misses. Serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart.

One serious near-miss had a PET of 0.0 s with a motorcycle travelling at 45.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 5.5%.
One serious near-miss had a PET of 1.1 s with a car travelling at 38.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 3.1%.
One serious near-miss had a PET of 0.7 s with a car travelling at 34.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 2.3%.
One serious near-miss had a PET of 1.4 s with a van travelling at 23.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.9%.

A car at 51.0 km/h was 1.5 s from a person, with adult death risk if hit of 9.0%.

A van at 23.8 km/h was 2.1 s from a person.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this crossing.
We offer to share the video for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We are writing about pedestrian safety outside our school at Park Avenue crossing. A Crossing Watch video measurement of 9.6 minutes (576.0 s) recorded 11 pedestrian crossings and 10 moving vehicles with an 85th percentile speed of 57.1 km/h. The drivers involved were speeding because they were late for work.

In that recording, 4 of 11 crossings had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 2 of 11 within 1.5 s.

The analysis identified 2 serious near-misses and 2 close passes. One serious near-miss involved a bus at 52.3 km/h with 0.0 s between the pedestrian and vehicle on the same spot.

Another serious near-miss involved a motorcycle at 28.2 km/h with 0.7 s between the pedestrian and vehicle on the same spot.

One close pass involved a car at 46.0 km/h with 2.1 s between the pedestrian and vehicle on the same spot.

Another close pass involved a bus at 56.5 km/h with 2.4 s between the pedestrian and vehicle on the same spot.

Based on Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15+ hit by car fronts, the estimated adult death risk if hit was 10.0% for the bus at 52.3 km/h and 1.3% for the motorcycle at 28.2 km/h, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.

Engineering context is limited because PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 9.6 minutes with 11 pedestrian crossings and 10 moving vehicles.

81.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 5 gaps, 1 of them 12 s or more, longest 74.1 s, with the first and last gaps cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce speeds and provide priority for pedestrians.

We can share the video and measurement data for your review and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the crossing on Market Street outside our school.

A video count of 4.4 minutes (264.0 s) recorded 7 pedestrian crossings and 8 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 58.5 km/h. Every person in these near-misses was a pupil of our school. Of the 7 crossings, 2 of 7 (1 in 3.5) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 1 of 7 (1 in 7) within 1.5 s.

One serious near-miss left 0.8 s between pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot and involved a car at 53.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 11.0% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second event was a close pass with 2.3 s between pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot and involved a bus at 12.3 km/h.

LETTER:
To the Road Authority,

We write concerning the crossing outside our school at Brook Street crossing.

We arranged video monitoring using SAM tracking with road-plane geometry. In 17.4 minutes we recorded 20 pedestrian crossings and 24 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 44.9 km/h. There were 2 serious near-misses where pedestrian and moving vehicle were on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 4 close passes between 1.5 s and 3.0 s.

The most severe event had a post-encroachment time of 0.7 s and involved a motorcycle. That motorcycle was travelling at 37.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 2.8%.

A second serious event had a post-encroachment time of 0.5 s and involved a car. That car was travelling at 17.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 0.5%.

A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.6 s and involved a bus. That bus was travelling at 22.4 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 0.6%.

A further close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.8 s and involved a motorcycle. That motorcycle was travelling at 22.8 km/h.

A final close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.5 s and involved a bus. That bus was travelling at 30.8 km/h. All risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosén & Sander 2009.

Engineering review noted PV² of 0.0 x 10^8 based on 69 pedestrians and 83 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 17.4 minutes of video, while a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can double-count. It also noted 56.4% of time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with 5 such gaps and longest 11.1 s, though the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. During the 17.4 minutes of observation there were 5 gaps of at least 6 s and the longest gap lasted 11.1 s.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with a speed table to reduce speeds and provide protected crossing time.

We are happy to share the video and underlying measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the crossing on Market Street outside our school.

A video count of 4.4 minutes (264.0 s) recorded 7 pedestrian crossings and 8 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 58.5 km/h. Among the worst near-misses measured, the fastest vehicle was going at 53.5 km/h. Of the 7 crossings, 2 of 7 (1 in 3.5) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 1 of 7 (1 in 7) within 1.5 s.

One serious near-miss left 0.8 s between pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot and involved a car at 53.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 11.0% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second event was a close pass with 2.3 s between pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot and involved a bus at 12.3 km/h.

For context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video, so this 4.4 minute count with 7 crossings and 8 vehicles is too short to assess those rates. Also, 85.3% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, based on 4 gaps with longest 10.0 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with a raised table to slow vehicles and give priority to pupils crossing.

We can share the video for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at River Lane crossing

Dear Sir or Madam,

On behalf of the school beside River Lane crossing, I write to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone with signs.

Crossing Watch video observation lasted 6.8 minutes (408.0 s). During that time 4 pedestrian crossings and 32 moving vehicles were counted. The 85th percentile speed was 39.7 km/h.

In that period there were 3 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass defined as 1.5 to 3.0 s apart. In 3 cases the pedestrian was first and in 1 case the vehicle was first.

One serious near-miss involved a car at 41.4 km/h with a separation of 0.8 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 4.0 percent, based on Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15 plus. At a 20 km/h limit the estimated impact would be 15.5 km/h with a death risk of 0.4 percent.

Another serious near-miss involved a car at 20.6 km/h with a separation of 1.0 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.6 percent. At a 20 km/h limit the estimated impact would be 20.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.6 percent.

One close pass involved a car at 16.0 km/h with a separation of 2.7 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.0 percent.

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about safety at the Station Road crossing outside our school.

In 9.3 minutes of video (558.0 s) we recorded 3 pedestrian crossings and 19 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 31.9 km/h. The counts above are past the threshold the road code sets for a zebra crossing. 3 of 3 crossings (1 in 1) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s, and 2 of 3 (1 in 1.5) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 29.2-100.0% and 9.4-99.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

There were 2 serious near-misses (less than 1.5 s apart) and 1 close pass (1.5-3.0 s). One serious near-miss had a car at 34.3 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.0 s. The modelled adult death risk if hit by the car front for that impact is 2.2%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). A second serious near-miss had a van at 30.8 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.3 s. The modelled adult death risk if hit by the car front for that impact is 1.6%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h. A close pass had a car at 14.6 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 2.6 s.

PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 9.3, with 3 pedestrian crossings and 19 moving vehicles counted. 50.9% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 10 gaps, 3 of them 12 s or more, longest 81.6 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce speeds and protect pupils.

We are happy to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority
Subject: Request for safety improvement at Ring Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school monitored the Ring Road crossing outside the school from video for 20.8 minutes (1248.0 s). In that time we recorded 32 crossings and 21 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 55.2 km/h. Parents see the same danger here at each school dismissal.

The analysis found 3 serious near-misses (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 1 close pass (1.5-3.0 s). Of the 4 interactions, 2 were person-first and 2 were vehicle-first.

One serious near-miss had a PET of 1.3 s with a car at 57.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed, the death risk is 15.1% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
Another serious near-miss had a PET of 1.3 s with a car at 36.4 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed, the death risk is 2.6%.
A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.8 s with a bus at 14.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed, the death risk is 0.4%.
One close pass had a PET of 2.5 s with a van at 30.2 km/h.

For engineering context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 (92 pedestrians and 61 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 20.8 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice: 1.3x the true count in our drone test). Also, 46.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps in total and 4 of them 12 s or more and longest 86.3 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We can share the video and Crossing Watch measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at River Lane crossing

Dear Sir or Madam,

On behalf of the school beside River Lane crossing, I write to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone with signs. Once this fix is built, no one will die at this crossing.

Crossing Watch video observation lasted 6.8 minutes (408.0 s). During that time 4 pedestrian crossings and 32 moving vehicles were counted. The 85th percentile speed was 39.7 km/h.

In that period there were 3 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass defined as 1.5 to 3.0 s apart. In 3 cases the pedestrian was first and in 1 case the vehicle was first.

One serious near-miss involved a car at 41.4 km/h with a separation of 0.8 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 4.0 percent, based on Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15 plus. At a 20 km/h limit the estimated impact would be 15.5 km/h with a death risk of 0.4 percent.

Another serious near-miss involved a car at 20.6 km/h with a separation of 1.0 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.6 percent. At a 20 km/h limit the estimated impact would be 20.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.6 percent.

A third serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 12.9 km/h with a separation of 0.3 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.3 percent. At a 20 km/h limit the estimated impact would be 12.9 km/h with a death risk of 0.3 percent.

One close pass involved a car at 16.0 km/h with a separation of 2.7 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.0 percent.

Regarding longer-term warrants, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 6.8. The share of time inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed was 95.7 percent, from 8 gaps of 6 s or more including 2 gaps of 12 s or more with the longest gap 83.4 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. For reference, the UK Traffic Signs Manual chapter 6, 13.5.2 notes that 4 to 6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds while other groups such as children may need 10 to 12 s or longer.

We request the raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone as a physical fix to lower speeds and create safe gaps. We are willing to share the full video and Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority
Subject: Request for safety improvement at Ring Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school monitored the Ring Road crossing outside the school from video for 20.8 minutes (1248.0 s). In that time we recorded 32 crossings and 21 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 55.2 km/h. Many of these drivers were not watching the road at all.

The analysis found 3 serious near-misses (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 1 close pass (1.5-3.0 s). Of the 4 interactions, 2 were person-first and 2 were vehicle-first.

One serious near-miss had a PET of 1.3 s with a car at 57.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed, the death risk is 15.1% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
Another serious near-miss had a PET of 1.3 s with a car at 36.4 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed, the death risk is 2.6%.
A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.8 s with a bus at 14.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed, the death risk is 0.4%.
One close pass had a PET of 2.5 s with a van at 30.2 km/h.

For engineering context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 (92 pedestrians and 61 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 20.8 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice: 1.3x the true count in our drone test). Also, 46.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps in total and 4 of them 12 s or more and longest 86.3 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We can share the video and Crossing Watch measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the crossing outside our school on Lantern Road. Crossing Watch video covering 42.7 minutes (2562.0 s) recorded 12 crossings and 20 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 50.0 km/h. This change is certain to save lives at this crossing.

In that period there were 2 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart.

1 close pass involved a motorcycle travelling at 25.7 km/h with 1.7 s between pedestrian and vehicle. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.6%.

At a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact speed would be 0.0 km/h for the 1.0 s serious near-miss and 20.0 km/h for the 0.7 s serious near-miss.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 17 pedestrians and 28 moving vehicles per hour scaled from 42.7 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice (1.3x in drone test). 88.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 12 gaps, 6 of them 12 s or more and longest 70.1 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We would be pleased to share the video and measurements to help your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvements at Cedar Lane crossing

We write concerning the crossing outside our school at Cedar Lane crossing. A video survey of 43.5 minutes (2610.0 s) recorded 22 crossings and 15 vehicles.

In that period, 3 of 22 crossings (1 in 7.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 2 of 22 (1 in 11) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 2.9-34.9% and 1.1-29.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The 85th percentile speed was 51.2 mph. Serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and close pass as 1.5-3.0 s. There were 2 serious near-misses and 1 close pass.

The most serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.4 s and involved an auto-rickshaw at 49.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 8.0% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+).

A second serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s and involved a bus at 12.0 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.3%.

A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.9 s and involved a car at 25.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.3%.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, based on 30 pedestrians and 21 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 43.5 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can double-count.

Also, 49.9% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 10 gaps, 4 of them 12 s or more, and the longest 84.8 s; the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We would be pleased to share the video and data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We write about the crossing outside our school on River Lane. Video measurements over 17.8 minutes recorded 5 crossings and 19 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 52.7 km/h. Several children have been hurt at this crossing since the term began.

In that period there was 1 serious near-miss and 4 close passes. A serious near-miss is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s apart. Of the 5 people, 1 crossed before the vehicle and 4 crossed after the vehicle, with 0 crossing at the same time.

The most serious near-miss had a gap of 1.3 s with a car travelling at 15.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.4% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A close pass had a gap of 1.9 s with an auto-rickshaw travelling at 34.5 km/h.

A second close pass had a gap of 1.8 s with a motorcycle travelling at 15.2 km/h.

A third close pass had a gap of 2.2 s with a car travelling at 24.4 km/h.

A fourth close pass had a gap of 2.7 s with a bus travelling at 50.3 km/h.

For context, PV² was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 17 pedestrians and 64 moving vehicles an hour, but this was scaled from 17.8 minutes of video whereas a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice. In the same video, 43.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 1 gap of 6 s or more and 1 gap of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 42.3 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and give pedestrians priority.

We can share the video and measurement files for your review and would welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We can share the video and measurement files for your review and would welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

A car at 43.2 km/h was 2.3 s from a person on the same spot; the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.3%.

Yours faithfully,

A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.8 s with a bus at 14.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed, the death risk is 0.4%.
One close pass had a PET of 2.5 s with a van at 30.2 km/h.

For engineering context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 (92 pedestrians and 61 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 20.8 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice: 1.3x the true count in our drone test). We request you install a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We can share the video and Crossing Watch measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvements at Cedar Lane crossing

We write concerning the crossing outside our school at Cedar Lane crossing. A video survey of 43.5 minutes (2610.0 s) recorded 22 crossings and 15 vehicles.

In that period, 3 of 22 crossings (1 in 7.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 2 of 22 (1 in 11) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 2.9-34.9% and 1.1-29.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The 85th percentile speed was 51.2 km/h. The closest of these near-misses was the fault of Mr. Tarun Mehra, who runs the tea stall. Serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and close pass as 1.5-3.0 s. There were 2 serious near-misses and 1 close pass.

The most serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.4 s and involved an auto-rickshaw at 49.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 8.0% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+).

A second serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s and involved a bus at 12.0 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.3%.

A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.9 s and involved a car at 25.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.3%.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, based on 30 pedestrians and 21 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 43.5 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can double-count.

Also, 49.9% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 10 gaps, 4 of them 12 s or more, and the longest 84.8 s; the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We would be pleased to share the video and data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside our school

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about pedestrian safety outside our school. A video review using SAM tracking and road-plane geometry measured the crossing for 37.5 minutes (2250.0 s). In that time 22 crossings and 20 vehicles were counted.

Of the 22 crossings, 3 of 22 (1 in 7.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 
Of the 22 crossings, 2 of 22 (1 in 11) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 1.5 s of the person. 
Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 2.9-34.9% and 1.1-29.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile vehicle speed was 61.3 km/h. By these figures the crossing already qualifies for a signal-controlled crossing.

The worst near-miss was a serious case with a car at 31.7 km/h passing 0.2 s from a person. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 1.7% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.

Yours faithfully,

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvements at Cedar Lane crossing

We write concerning the crossing outside our school at Cedar Lane crossing. A video survey of 43.5 minutes (2610.0 s) recorded 22 crossings and 15 vehicles.

In that period, 3 of 22 crossings (1 in 7.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 2 of 22 (1 in 11) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 2.9-34.9% and 1.1-29.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The 85th percentile speed was 51.2 km/h. This is what happens at the crossing on each day of the school week. Serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and close pass as 1.5-3.0 s. There were 2 serious near-misses and 1 close pass.

The most serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.4 s and involved an auto-rickshaw at 49.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 8.0% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+).

A second serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s and involved a bus at 12.0 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.3%.

A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.9 s and involved a car at 25.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.3%.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, based on 30 pedestrians and 21 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 43.5 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can double-count.

Also, 49.9% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 10 gaps, 4 of them 12 s or more, and the longest 84.8 s; the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We would be pleased to share the video and data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at River Lane crossing

Dear Sir or Madam,

On behalf of the school beside River Lane crossing, I write to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone with signs. The closest of these near-misses was the fault of Mr. Tarun Mehra, who runs the tea stall.

Crossing Watch video observation lasted 6.8 minutes (408.0 s). During that time 4 pedestrian crossings and 32 moving vehicles were counted. The 85th percentile speed was 39.7 km/h.

In that period there were 3 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass defined as 1.5 to 3.0 s apart. In 3 cases the pedestrian was first and in 1 case the vehicle was first.

One serious near-miss involved a car at 41.4 km/h with a separation of 0.8 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 4.0 percent, based on Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15 plus. At a 20 km/h limit the estimated impact would be 15.5 km/h with a death risk of 0.4 percent.

Another serious near-miss involved a car at 20.6 km/h with a separation of 1.0 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.6 percent. At a 20 km/h limit the estimated impact would be 20.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.6 percent.

A third serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 12.9 km/h with a separation of 0.3 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.3 percent. At a 20 km/h limit the estimated impact would be 12.9 km/h with a death risk of 0.3 percent.

One close pass involved a car at 16.0 km/h with a separation of 2.7 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.0 percent.

Regarding longer-term warrants, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 6.8. The share of time inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed was 95.7 percent, from 8 gaps of 6 s or more including 2 gaps of 12 s or more with the longest gap 83.4 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. For reference, the UK Traffic Signs Manual chapter 6, 13.5.2 notes that 4 to 6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds while other groups such as children may need 10 to 12 s or longer.

We request the raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone as a physical fix to lower speeds and create safe gaps. We are willing to share the full video and Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside the school

Dear Sir/Madam,

We asked for measurements at the Ring Road crossing. In 28.9 minutes 8 people were seen crossing and 12 vehicles were counted.

The headline finding is that 6 of 8 crossings (1 in 1.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 4 of 8 (1 in 2) within 1.5 s.

If this recording is typical the exact 95% ranges are 34.9-96.8% of crossings within 3 s and 15.7-84.3% within 1.5 s. In this recording serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass means 1.5-3.0 s apart.

The 85th percentile speed was 61.2 km/h. In the near-miss with a time gap of 1.4 s the vehicle was going at 40.3 km/h, and in the one with a time gap of 0.9 s it was going at 44.5 km/h. One serious near-miss had a PET of 1.4 s with a car at 44.5 km/h; the adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 5.2% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

A second serious near-miss had a PET of 0.9 s with a car at 40.3 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 3.6%.

A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.2 s with a van at 31.3 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 1.7%.

A fourth serious near-miss had a PET of 0.6 s with a bus at 19.4 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 0.6%.

A close pass had a PET of 1.6 s with a car at 14.4 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 0.3%.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 when scaled from 28.9 minutes to 17 pedestrians and 25 vehicles an hour, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount pedestrians by 1.3x. Also 73.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location.

We are happy to share the underlying video and measurements for review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority
Subject: Request for safety improvement at Ring Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school monitored the Ring Road crossing outside the school from video for 20.8 minutes (1248.0 s). In that time we recorded 32 crossings and 21 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 55.2 km/h. Children hit at these speeds face a far higher risk of death than adults.

The analysis found 3 serious near-misses (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 1 close pass (1.5-3.0 s). Of the 4 interactions, 2 were person-first and 2 were vehicle-first.

One serious near-miss had a PET of 1.3 s with a car at 57.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed, the death risk is 15.1% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
Another serious near-miss had a PET of 1.3 s with a car at 36.4 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed, the death risk is 2.6%.
A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.8 s with a bus at 14.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed, the death risk is 0.4%.
One close pass had a PET of 2.5 s with a van at 30.2 km/h.

For engineering context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 (92 pedestrians and 61 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 20.8 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice: 1.3x the true count in our drone test). Also, 46.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps in total and 4 of them 12 s or more and longest 86.3 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We can share the video and Crossing Watch measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about safety at the Orchard Lane crossing. Crossing Watch monitoring (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) for 18.0 minutes recorded 5 pedestrian crossings and 5 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 46.5 km/h. Several children have been hurt at this crossing since the term began.

We identified 2 serious near-misses (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 2 close passes (1.5-3.0 s). In 3 cases the person reached the conflict point first and in 1 case the vehicle did.

1 serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 43.2 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.5 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 4.7% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+), compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.

1 serious near-miss involved a van at 34.1 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.1 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 2.1%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.

1 close pass involved a motorcycle at 22.7 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 2.4 s.

1 close pass involved a car at 34.4 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 2.6 s.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 (17 pedestrians and 17 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 18.0 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount by 1.3x). 89.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed (4 gaps of 6 s or more, 4 of 12 s or more, longest 80.0 s; the first and last gaps are cut short by the video).

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location to lower speeds and provide pedestrian priority.

We can share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Garden Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school asked for a video review of Garden Road crossing. Measurements were made by Crossing Watch using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time over 18.1 minutes, which is 1086.0 s, during which 11 crossings and 26 vehicles were observed.

In that recording, 4 of 11 crossings (1 in 2.8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 4 of 11 (1 in 2.8) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 10.9-69.2% and 10.9-69.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.1-10.2 and 1.1-10.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile speed was 59.2 km/h. Of the 4 serious near-misses, defined as less than 1.5 s apart, 1 was person-first, 2 were vehicle-first and 1 was both at once.

The most severe serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.0 s with a van at 54.0 km/h and an adult death risk if hit of 11.5%, based on Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15+ hit by a car front. At a 20 km/h limit the estimated impact would be 0.0 km/h with death risk 0.0%.

A second serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.5 s with a car at 52.1 km/h and an adult death risk if hit of 9.9%. At a 20 km/h limit the estimated impact would be 20.0 km/h with death risk 0.6%.

A third serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.1 s with a van at 50.6 km/h and an adult death risk if hit of 8.7%. At a 20 km/h limit the estimated impact would be 20.0 km/h with death risk 0.6%.

A fourth serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.0 s with an auto-rickshaw at 28.1 km/h and an adult death risk if hit of 1.2%. At a 20 km/h limit the estimated impact would be 20.0 km/h with death risk 0.6%.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, scaled from 18.1 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and that broken tracks can count one twice. In the video, 50.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 1 gap of 6 s or more and 1 of 12 s or more and longest gap 67.8 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you provide a raised zebra crossing with speed table at Garden Road crossing to reduce speeds and give pedestrians priority. Most of these near misses involved speeding school buses during the morning rush.

We are willing to share the video and measurement files for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Road Authority,

We write about the crossing on River Lane. In 3.6 minutes we counted 6 pedestrian crossings and 46 moving vehicles.

6 of 6 crossings (1 in 1) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 6 (1 in 2) had a vehicle within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 54.1-100.0% and 11.8-88.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The 85th percentile speed was 54.1 km/h. These results satisfy the official criteria for a pedestrian signal at this spot.

Worst near-misses recorded were:
A serious near-miss with a motorcycle at 51.9 km/h had 1.1 s between the person and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is estimated at 9.8% (Rosen & Sander 2009, adults 15+).
A serious near-miss with a car at 19.5 km/h had 1.3 s between the person and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is estimated at 0.6%.
A serious near-miss with a motorcycle at 14.0 km/h had 1.4 s between the person and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is estimated at 0.4%.
A close pass with a car at 39.1 km/h had 1.9 s between the person and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is estimated at 1.2%.
A close pass with a car at 16.3 km/h had 1.6 s between the person and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is estimated at 0.3%.

Engineering context is limited. PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 3.6 minutes. Counted was 6 pedestrian crossings and 46 moving vehicles.
88.3% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 11 gaps, 4 of them 12 s or more, longest 51.9 s. The first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce speeds and provide protected priority.

We are happy to share the measurement file and discuss the results further.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Garden Road crossing

Our school asked for a video review of Garden Road crossing. Measurements were made by Crossing Watch using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time over 18.1 minutes, which is 1086.0 s, during which 11 crossings and 26 vehicles were observed.

In that recording, 4 of 11 crossings (1 in 2.8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 4 of 11 (1 in 2.8) within 1.5 s. The 85th percentile speed was 59.2 km/h. Parents see the same danger here at each school dismissal. Of the 4 serious near-misses, defined as less than 1.5 s apart, 1 was person-first, 2 were vehicle-first and 1 was both at once.

The most severe serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.0 s with a van at 54.0 km/h and an adult death risk if hit of 11.5%, based on Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15+ hit by a car front. At a 20 km/h limit the estimated impact would be 0.0 km/h with death risk 0.0%.

A second serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.5 s with a car at 52.1 km/h and an adult death risk if hit of 9.9%. At a 20 km/h limit the estimated impact would be 20.0 km/h with death risk 0.6%.

A third serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.1 s with a van at 50.6 km/h and an adult death risk if hit of 8.7%. At a 20 km/h limit the estimated impact would be 20.0 km/h with death risk 0.6%.

A fourth serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.0 s with an auto-rickshaw at 28.1 km/h and an adult death risk if hit of 1.2%. At a 20 km/h limit the estimated impact would be 20.0 km/h with death risk 0.6%.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, scaled from 18.1 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and that broken tracks can count one twice. In the video, 50.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 1 gap of 6 s or more and 1 of 12 s or more and longest gap 67.8 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you provide a raised zebra crossing with speed table at Garden Road crossing to reduce speeds and give pedestrians priority.

We are willing to share the video and measurement files for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning safety outside our school at Bridge Street crossing.

A 5.0 minute (300.0 s) recording counted 5 pedestrian crossings and 20 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 55.4 km/h. In one of these events the vehicle struck the pedestrian.

1 close pass had PET of 2.7 s with a car at 38.4 km/h.

1 close pass had PET of 2.7 s with a car at 33.3 km/h.

PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 5.0 minutes.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with 20 km/h speed table and signs at this location.

We are happy to share the recording data and video for your review and to discuss next steps.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvements at Cedar Lane crossing

We write concerning the crossing outside our school at Cedar Lane crossing. A video survey of 43.5 minutes (2610.0 s) recorded 22 crossings and 15 vehicles.

In that period, 3 of 22 crossings (1 in 7.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 2 of 22 (1 in 11) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 2.9-34.9% and 1.1-29.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The 85th percentile speed was 51.2 km/h. In the near-miss with a time gap of 0.4 s the vehicle was going at 49.5 km/h, and in the one with a time gap of 1.2 s it was going at 12.0 km/h. Serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and close pass as 1.5-3.0 s. There were 2 serious near-misses and 1 close pass.

The most serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.4 s and involved an auto-rickshaw at 49.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 8.0% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+).

A second serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s and involved a bus at 12.0 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.3%.

A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.9 s and involved a car at 25.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.3%.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, based on 30 pedestrians and 21 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 43.5 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can double-count.

Also, 49.9% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 10 gaps, 4 of them 12 s or more, and the longest 84.8 s; the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We would be pleased to share the video and data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

The bus in that close pass was at 33.4 km/h.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the School Lane crossing on behalf of the school. A video of 7.8 minutes (468.0 s) was analysed by Crossing Watch using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time. In that period there were 6 pedestrian crossings and 23 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 54.5 km/h. To sum up, the recording showed 2 serious near-misses and 3 close passes.

For context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this video is 7.8 minutes. In the video 86.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed. There were 10 gaps of 6 s or more, 2 of them 12 s or more, with the longest gap 21.1 s. The first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

The analysis found 2 serious near-misses and 3 close passes. Serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart. Close pass is 1.5 to 3.0 s.

One serious near-miss had a time gap of 0.0 s with a bus at 37.4 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front the death risk at that speed is 2.8%. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would be 20.0 km/h with an adult death risk of 0.6%.

A second serious near-miss had a time gap of 0.8 s with a bus at 17.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front the death risk at that speed is 0.5%. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would be 17.8 km/h with an adult death risk of 0.5%. Risk figures are from Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15+ hit by car fronts.

A close pass had a time gap of 2.1 s with an auto-rickshaw at 54.7 km/h.

A close pass had a time gap of 2.7 s with a car at 19.6 km/h.

A close pass had a time gap of 2.9 s with a car at 14.5 km/h.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for children and other pedestrians crossing to school.

We are happy to share the video and the full measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Brook Street crossing

I write as head of the school beside Brook Street crossing. A video survey by Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) measured 7 pedestrian crossings and 34 moving vehicles in 4.9 minutes (294.0 s).

The 85th percentile speed was 59.4 km/h. Regarding gaps, 43.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 11 gaps, 3 of them 12 s or more, longest 58.4 s. The first and last gaps are cut short by the video. PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this recording is 4.9 minutes, so those rates are not reported.

We recorded 3 serious near-misses (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 2 close passes (1.5-3.0 s). Arrival order was 1 person first, 3 vehicle first and 1 both at once.

The worst cases were:
One serious near-miss had a PET of 0.0 s with an auto-rickshaw at 17.6 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.5% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.
A second serious near-miss had a PET of 1.2 s with an auto-rickshaw at 18.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.5%.
A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.7 s with an auto-rickshaw at 13.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.3%.
One close pass had a PET of 1.8 s with a car at 57.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 8.1%.
One close pass had a PET of 2.8 s with a car at 50.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.0%.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone with signs at Brook Street crossing.

We are willing to share the video and data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the safety of the crossing outside our school at the North Avenue crossing.

In 43.7 minutes of video we recorded 23 crossings and 8 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 54.6 km/h. This change is certain to save lives at this crossing. 2 of 23 crossings (1 in 12) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 1 of 23 crossings (1 in 23) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 1.5 s. If this recording is typical, the exact 95% ranges are 1.1-28.0% and 0.1-21.9% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 0.2-7.2 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The most serious near-miss involved a motorcycle at 48.8 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.1 s. An adult hit by a car front at that speed would face a 7.5% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact speed of 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.

A second close pass involved a car at 53.3 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 2.2 s. An adult hit by a car front at that speed would face a 1.6% death risk, compared with 0.0% at 0.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 32 pedestrians and 11 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 43.7 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour. 95.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with 9 such gaps and longest 7.6 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and speed table at this location.

We have the video measurements and are ready to share them to help your assessment. Please let us know how to proceed.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We write concerning the crossing outside our school at Brook Street crossing.

We arranged video monitoring using SAM tracking with road-plane geometry. In 17.4 minutes we recorded 20 pedestrian crossings and 24 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 44.9 km/h. A further close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.8 s and involved a motorcycle. That motorcycle was travelling at 22.8 km/h.

A final close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.5 s and involved a bus. That bus was travelling at 30.8 km/h. All risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosén & Sander 2009.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with a speed table to reduce speeds and provide protected crossing time. Parents told us that children are often left to cross alone after lunch.

We are happy to share the video and underlying measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Ring Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

I write on behalf of the school located at the Ring Road crossing to request a safety improvement.

We commissioned a video review of the crossing. During 4.0 minutes (240.0 s) of video, 3 pedestrian crossings and 13 moving vehicles were counted. The 85th percentile speed was 49.5 km/h.

No serious near-misses (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) were recorded. There were 2 close passes (1.5-3.0 s apart).

The first close pass involved a van at 16.8 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 1.9 s.

The second close pass involved a bus at 45.4 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 2.7 s.

For adults hit by a car front, Rosén & Sander 2009 estimates the adult death risk if hit in these incidents would have been 0.0% for the van and 0.0% for the bus, and 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit. If a 7-year-old had been hit by the bus at 45.4 km/h, the chance of death would have been about 15%.

The engineering note advises that PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this video is 4.0 minutes.

In this video 63.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps of 6 s or more and 6 of 12 s or more, the longest 81.9 s. The note states the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds, while other groups such as children may need 10-12 s or longer.

We therefore request installation of a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We are willing to share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements to support your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal
